title: KV cache prefetch thresholds and prefix churn troubleshooting - StellarWare deep dive
summary: Deep technical session to diagnose frequent KV cache evictions and high paging on StellarWare's private deployment. Focus areas: prefetch thresholds, prefix reuse hot spots, long-context handling, and tradeoffs with batching and quantization in VPC/on-prem setups.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sam Ortega (StellarWare Eng Lead), Maya Chen (StellarWare SRE), Liam O'Neill (StellarWare CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Customers seeing repeated KV evictions during long multi-turn sessions; paging spikes when prefix hotspots collide; prefetch heuristic currently too conservative for their workload; latency SLOs missed once paging begins.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate, auto-transcript quality: medium) ---
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone thanks for carving out the time. quick agenda: reproduce the eviction pattern, review telemetry, walk prefetch tuning, and outline a pilot.
[00:28] Sam: Yeah thanks. We've been hitting this with our support chat flows — long 6-10 turn conversations, sometimes a bunch of repeated prefixes when customers paste logs. It looks like the KV cache gets evicted mid-conversation and latency jumps to like 2x.
[00:45] Priya (SE): Got it. when you say "evicted" are you seeing full-kv drop or partial, like some prefixes still in mem?
[00:55] Maya: It's weird — there are prefixes that stay hot but some older tokens get paged out, then the model takes a hit while it repopulates. We see spike in disk iops and CPU.
[01:12] Priya: ok so likely a combination of prefix churn and thresholding. Quick refresher: Redwood's runtime tries to keep recent KV chunks pinned based on the LRU-ish scoring but with a prefetched headroom. If headroom is too small for your multi-turn distribution we will evict earlier and pay the paging penalty.
[01:35] Sam: Right, and we noticed that when multiple sessions reuse similar prefixes (for example the "stacktrace:" token blob), the reuse causes collision and some sessions lose their prefix.
[01:50] Priya: that's prefix reuse collision — two different session IDs map to the same prefix bucket in the in-memory store when prefix hashing is overloaded, especially under heavy concurrency. We have mitigation knobs: increase prefix table size, tune prefix fingerprinting, and adjust prefetch thresholds per-model.
[02:10] Liam (CTO): Before we dive knobs, what's the risk if we simply bump the in-memory allocation? We're on-prem so we can allocate more RAM.
[02:22] Priya: Increasing memory helps, yes, but it changes batching behavior and can increase GC or numa effects on certain hardware. Also if your model uses 32-bit kv keys vs compacted keys the absolute memory usage varies.
[02:38] Maya: Also network considerations — our VPC private link has some bandwidth caps, and paging causes extra network traffic when we spill to NFS. we noticed egress when the paging moves to a remote store.
[02:55] Alex: good callout. for on-prem/VPC customers, we recommend local SSD-backed paging nodes to avoid networked paging. Do you have local NVMe on the inference hosts?
[03:06] Sam: yes, each node has NVMe but it's sometimes saturated during peak.
[03:12] Priya: ok. a few concrete things we'll look at: 1) prefetch headroom (% of KV allocated to read-ahead), 2) eviction policy tweak (LRU->LFU hybrid), 3) prefix table size, and 4) batching heuristics that affect how long active KV stays warm.
[03:33] Sam: can you explain "prefetch headroom" in practical terms? we tried changing some flags but results were noisy.
[03:40] Priya: sure — we maintain a sliding window of recently used prefixes plus a prefetch buffer that anticipates next tokens. headroom is basically the buffer size expressed as a percent of max KV cache. if it's too low we avoid prefetch and then miss, if it's too high we evict other useful prefixes. for chat flows with predictable next tokens, higher headroom improves latency.
[04:02] Maya: but that increased memory means we saw less effective batching because requests took more resident memory? I think we saw throughput drop at times.
[04:12] Priya: there is a throughput vs latency tradeoff. Increasing headroom increases per-session memory, reducing the concurrent sessions per GPU. If your latency SLO is strict you can sacrifice concurrency. we should compute session working set size.
[04:28] Alex: we can run a benchmark to map headroom -> concurrency -> p50/p95. we'll produce a small matrix.
[04:36] Liam: what's the guidance on long-context token pinning? we have very long contexts for some customers (20k tokens).
[04:44] Priya: we have a 'pin list' feature — you can mark long-context prefixes (like conversation starter or system prompts) as pinned so they're never evicted. downside: pins increase memory pressure. for 20k contexts we recommend selective pinning (only the first N tokens that are frequently re-referenced), and rolling checkpointing for older segments.
[05:07] Sam: is there an automated way to infer which prefixes to pin? manual is tough.
[05:12] Priya: yes, we can run workload sampling via telemetry to find high-reuse prefixes and propose pin candidates. that's part of Redwood Optimize. we can run that on your anonymized traces if you approve.
[05:23] Maya: we are fine sharing anonymized traces — will need a DPA.
[05:27] Alex: we'll send the security docs and DPA link after the call.
[05:32] Priya: another factor: quantization. When you quantize weights aggressively, inference is faster but we sometimes see slightly different KV patterns because the tokenization/attention length distribution shifts a little. This is subtle but in tight SLOs it matters.
[05:50] Sam: interesting — so quantization could indirectly change what ends up in the KV window?
[05:55] Priya: yes, model compute changes can alter effective token latency and batching windows. we saw cases where Q4_0 vs Q8_0 changed prompt latency and thus overlapping concurrent lookups.
[06:08] Maya: we also run different batch sizes across A/B groups; could that cause prefix collision?
[06:13] Priya: batch sizing affects how long a request waits in queue and can change cache warmup behavior. small batches favor latency, large batches improve throughput but can increase the chances of eviction in between micro-batches.
[06:29] Sam: ok. what about the eviction algorithm - you mentioned LFU hybrid - how do we decide?
[06:36] Priya: LFU helps when you have stable hotspots; LRU favors recency. hybrid tries to keep stable hot prefixes while allowing short-term recency. We can experiment with a decay factor on counts so the system adapts to changes in reuse.
[06:53] Liam: what's the rollback if a change breaks things? can we do canary on a fraction of traffic?
[06:57] Alex: yes, Redwood Console supports rollout policies and canary. we can do 10% traffic with modified prefetch headroom and collect telemetry for an hour then revert.
[07:10] Maya: telemetry — which metrics should we focus on during the run?
[07:14] Priya: p50/p95 latency, KV hit rate, page-in iops, avg KV residency time, memory usage per process, and prefix collision counts. We'll add custom tags for your session ids so you can split by workflow.
[07:30] Sam: collision counts? how are those computed?
[07:33] Priya: we track prefix fingerprint collisions and sessions that reference the same physical bucket; it's a count metric exposed in the runtime telemetry. high cluster-wide counts suggest the prefix table is undersized.
[07:48] Alex: quick note — because you're on-prem using our private package, you can increase the prefix table size in config and restart the runtime; no code changes. but there is a rolling restart cost.
[07:59] Sam: What's the config key? we changed "kv.prefetch_headroom" but maybe missed the prefix table key.
[08:06] Priya: correct key is kv.prefix_table_size and kv.prefetch_headroom_pct. We'll send exact config snippets.
[08:12] Sam: great.
[08:15] [08:15] (transcription noise) Speaker overlap for a few seconds; Sam talking over Priya.
[08:30] Priya: another edge-case: when a prefix includes very large embedded blobs (like pasted logs) we sometimes treat them as unique prefixes every session; this bloats the prefix index. For those we recommend content hashing with normalization or applying a size cutoff and storing only a short fingerprint.
[08:55] Maya: that's likely what we have — customers paste 4k+ character logs at times.
[09:02] Priya: set normalization rules to trim repeated patterns and store shorter fingerprints. We'll provide examples.
[09:12] Liam: any guidance about SSD vs NVMe for paging?
[09:17] Priya: NVMe local SSD is strongly recommended; the runtime assumes low latency paging. network attached storage is fallback but will degrade p95 significantly. also choose devices with sustained write IOPS.
[09:31] Alex: ok, let's talk about an action plan and a pilot. We'll run a 3-phase pilot: 1) telemetry sampling + pin candidate generation, 2) small canary with prefetch headroom adjustments and prefix_table_size bump, 3) broader pilot with pinning & config tuning.
[09:49] Sam: timeline?
[09:51] Alex: phase 1 — 5 days to collect samples and propose pins; phase 2 — 2 days to run canary and observe; phase 3 — 1 week rollout. we can compress if you want.
[10:01] Maya: we want concrete numbers for headroom vs concurrency.
[10:05] Priya: we'll produce a matrix and baseline script.
[10:10] Sam: what about saving snapshots of KV to accelerate warmup across restarts?
[10:16] Priya: yes, we support snapshotting hot prefixes to disk and preloading on startup. for on-prem this reduces warmup time but increases start-up IO. Good for stateful nodes.
[10:28] Liam: any security concerns with snapshot files? encryption?
[10:31] Priya: snapshots can be encrypted with KMS/HSM in your environment. we'll document the config for encrypted snapshots.
[10:40] Alex: quick practical tuning recommendation right now: increase kv.prefix_table_size by 25%, set kv.prefetch_headroom_pct to 30% from your current 12% (example), enable sampling for top-100 prefixes for 48 hours, and hold pins only for top-10 candidates. Those are starting points not final.
[11:05] Sam: we'll try that in staging.
[11:08] Maya: what's the rollback time if we revert prefix_table_size?
[11:12] Priya: it's a restart; depending on your orchestrator 2-3 minutes per node; we recommend rolling restart so no outage.
[11:20] Sam: fine.
[11:22] Priya: final thing — batching heuristics: for your workload we recommend adaptive batching with a small max latency cap. this tries to preserve latency SLO while increasing micro-batching when traffic permits. we'll share our tuned policy.
[11:40] Alex: ok let's summarize next steps.
[11:44] [11:44] (auto-generated action list)
[11:45] Sam: one quick question — do you have known incompatibilities with our older NVIDIA driver on-prem? we run 520.x for now.
[11:52] Priya: some kernel-level GPU memcpy optimizations require newer drivers (535+); older drivers still work but may have higher CPU overhead for KV disk ops. We'll put exact driver guidance in the doc.
[12:08] Liam: good to know.
[12:10] Alex: ok that's it from us. we'll follow up with the security pack and the config snippets. thanks everyone.
